comments.author: @HiddenCanada
comments.text:
What do you think actually happened here, did decades of logs slowly build into a floating island, did high water tear part of the shoreline loose, or was it a mix of both? The strangest part to me is that Sentinel-2 imagery shows the island drifting across the reservoir before anyone had fully tracked where it went. 👀

If you’ve ever seen anything unusual on Williston Reservoir, I’d love to hear about it.

comments.author: @AWM-r8e
comments.text: Ooze Lake in Algonquin Park is full of floating peat

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: That’s a great comparison! Ooze Lake really does have floating mats of peat and vegetation that can look like little islands. The Williston Reservoir example was on a much bigger scale, but it’s fascinating that the same basic phenomenon shows up elsewhere in Canada too. Have you actually paddled through Ooze Lake?

replies.author: @JosephLevison-f9b
replies.text: ​@HiddenCanadaThere is a log that is kept every day. Birth pains before labor.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: I haven’t seen any evidence connecting tremors to this particular event. comments.text: Iirc it is known to move but they lost track of it for a while.

replies.author: @andrewbrown6522
replies.text:
​@HiddenCanadaNot sure if I have any river videos up right now but I fly it pretty often with a drone. The amount of sub channels is dizzying, even though I've been through many by kayak or boat.  

 I've often wondered how long it takes to "become land". We also have methane or something that comes up creating pockets which I imagine can become large voids under that new land. 

 On the floating island I seem to recall a FB from a local saying they must have boated by it several times while it was pinned on shore but they never noticed.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: That makes sense. The same kind of woody debris can behave very differently depending on the current and where it collects. In this case it may have helped form a floating vegetated mass, but in a river a big log jam can become a serious flood hazard very quickly, especially after a major storm or high-water event. Nature can rearrange a lot of material in a hurry.

replies.author: @andrewbrown6522
replies.text:
Where i live, the rivers fill areas with logs which block the flow and eventually fill in or break apart or fill in and break apart. 

 Big weather events can suddenly put everyone here at risk because the logs could rearrange into a full blockage and flood us.

replies.author: @Tucker1234567891
replies.text: I came here to say the same thing. I live on Lake Scugog in Ontario and I have seen smaller things like thiw before, they float up on my shoreline in the spring. Around here the ice rips ground from the swamp areas and it will float out to the lake. This spring there was like a 10 foot round one.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Exactly, what you’ve seen sounds like the same basic process on a much smaller scale. Logs and vegetation can bind together into floating mats, sometimes carrying grass and small trees with them. What made this one so unusual was the sheer size of it and the fact that it travelled about 30 kilometres. Nature gets pretty creative 😄
